rational-simplify.why: A rational expression is a fraction with polynomials in it, and it simplifies the same way numerical fractions do: factor, then cancel common *factors*. The extra care it needs is over excluded values — the inputs that would make the denominator zero.
traps: You may cancel factors, never terms. Crossing an ~x~ out of ~\f{x + 3}{x}~ is wrong.
State exclusions from the **original** denominator. A factor that cancels still breaks the expression at that value.

rational-mult-div.why: Multiplying rational expressions is multiply-across, and dividing is multiply by the reciprocal — exactly as with numbers. The only new skill is factoring everything first, so the common factors are visible before you multiply.
traps: Cancel before multiplying, not after. It keeps the numbers small and the work short.
Flip only the second fraction when dividing, and only after rewriting as a multiplication.

rational-add-sub.why: Adding rational expressions needs a common denominator, for exactly the reason ~\f{1}{2} + \f{1}{3}~ does: you cannot add parts of different sizes. The least common denominator is the product of all distinct factors, each to its highest power.
traps: ~\f{1}{a} + \f{1}{b}~ is **not** ~\f{1}{a+b}~. Test it with numbers once and you will never do it again.
Distribute the minus sign across the whole numerator when subtracting.

rational-equations.why: Multiplying through by the denominators clears the fractions and leaves an ordinary equation. But that step can create solutions that do not belong to the original, because you multiplied by something that might be zero — which is why checking is part of the method.
traps: Always test each answer in the **original** equation. A value that makes a denominator zero is extraneous and must be thrown out, even though the algebra produced it.

radical-operations.why: Radicals behave like terms with a common factor: ~3sqrt{2} + 5sqrt{2} = 8sqrt{2}~, while ~sqrt{2} + sqrt{3}~ cannot be combined at all. Simplifying first — pulling out square factors — is what reveals whether two radicals are actually alike.
traps: ~sqrt{a + b}~ is not ~sqrt{a} + sqrt{b}~. Check with 9 and 16: 5 against 7.
Roots multiply and divide freely under one sign, but they do not add or subtract that way.

radical-equations.why: Squaring both sides removes a square root, which is the only way in. But squaring is not reversible — it turns both ~3~ and ~-3~ into ~9~ — so it can manufacture false answers. Checking every candidate in the original equation is part of solving, not a courtesy.
traps: A radical equals a negative has no solution, because the radical sign means the positive root. Spot that before squaring.
Isolate the radical before squaring, or you will square a sum and make things worse.

rational-exponents.why: A fractional exponent is a root: the denominator is the root and the numerator is the power, so ~x^{2/3}~ is the cube root of ~x^{2}~. This notation matters because the ordinary exponent laws then apply to roots too, which radical notation hides.
traps: Take the root first, then the power — the numbers stay far smaller. ~64^{2/3}~ is ~4^{2} = 16~, not ~sqrt[3]{4096}~ computed the hard way.
A negative fractional exponent still means a reciprocal: ~x^{-1/2} = \f{1}{sqrt{x}}~.
